summary: A summary of the Process for Organization of Internet Standards Working Group, starting with events that led to its formation and continuing to the end of 1992. It was prepared in January 1993. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A history of a group formed to improve how the Internet's rules get made.

subtitle: Redesigning how the Internet standards community makes decisions.

tldr.problem: By 1992, the Internet standards process was under stress; decisions about IP addressing, the role of the IAB, and selection of leaders needed community input, but the process was unclear and communication broke down.
tldr.mechanism: The POISED working group studied the standards-making process and proposed a new system: IESG handles standards actions, leaders are nominated by a committee of volunteers, and a recall mechanism was added to improve accountability.
tldr.outcome: The standards process was reformed with explicit procedures for selecting IAB and IESG members, establishing community representation and formal terms of service.

today: RFC 1640 is an Informational RFC describing the 1992-1993 governance reform. The selection process it describes became the foundation for how the IETF has chosen its leaders ever since, establishing norms of community input and formal procedures that remain influential today.

sections.title: The Crisis in Internet Governance
sections.content:
By 1991, the Internet faced two urgent technical problems: the IP address space was running out, and routing tables were growing too large. These issues forced difficult architectural decisions, but the process for making them was unclear. The ROAD Working Group studied the issues, but bigger questions emerged: Who decides what? How should the IAB guide versus decide? When the IAB sent recommendations in June 1992, many people interpreted them as final decisions rather than discussion starters, creating conflict.

The Internet community had grown too large for informal leadership. The IAB and IESG existed, but members were selected through unclear processes, and there was no direct community voice in choosing them. These governance problems had to be fixed alongside the technical ones.
sections.eli5: The Internet got big, and people who made decisions had no clear process. Some thought the IAB was running things; others thought working groups should. Nobody really agreed on who had the authority to decide.

sections.title: The POISED Working Group
sections.content:
In August 1992, Vint Cerf, president of the Internet Society, called for a working group to examine the standards process. The POISED Working Group (Process for Organization of Internet Standards and Development, shortened to fit the database) was formed with Steve Crocker as chair. The group had three key questions: How should IAB and IESG members be chosen? How should disagreements among these groups be resolved? How could the community ensure fair hearing for all interests?

During August through November, the group conducted extensive email discussions (estimated at 20 MB), with proposals ranging from keeping the existing structure with reforms to completely replacing the IAB and IESG with two new boards. By mid-November, enough consensus had emerged to present options to the community.
sections.eli5: Steve Crocker led a big email discussion where people debated how to pick leaders and who gets to vote. Some wanted to change everything; others wanted small fixes.

sections.title: Reaching Consensus at the November IETF
sections.content:
The November 1992 IETF meeting in Washington, D.C. was the turning point. The intense discussions led to convergence on two key points. First, the IESG would make all standards actions decisions, bringing the decision point closer to working groups and shortening the cycle. Second, and more importantly, a new selection process emerged: a nomination committee of seven community volunteers would propose IAB and IESG members, with final ratification by the IAB and Internet Society trustees respectively.

The nomination committee would consist of seven members selected by lot from volunteers who had attended at least two IETF meetings. This requirement ensured familiarity with the community without creating formal membership rules. Terms would be two years, staggered so half of each body's membership was chosen each year.
sections.eli5: At the big IETF meeting in Washington, people finally agreed: a lottery pick from volunteers would nominate the leaders, and there would be a way to remove someone who wasn't working out.

sections.title: The New Selection and Recall System
sections.content:
The selected nomination committee members would propose candidates for each open position. If the committee could not reach consensus on a single candidate, it could forward multiple nominations to the ratifying body (the IAB for IESG candidates, the Internet Society for IAB candidates). Accountability was added through a recall mechanism: any community member could file a complaint with an ombudsman appointed by the Internet Society. If the complaint could not be resolved, a recall committee, randomly selected from volunteers, would consider it. A two-thirds vote by the recall committee could remove someone from office.

This design balanced community input with stability. Leaders served fixed terms, nominees had to pass community scrutiny, but no individual or faction could veto decisions. The random selection of both nomination and recall committees reduced the chance of entrenched power structures.
sections.eli5: Any community member could complain if a leader wasn't doing their job. A randomly chosen jury of volunteers would vote on whether to remove them.

sections.title: Approval and Implementation
sections.content:
The Internet Society trustees met in December 1992 and expressed strong approval for the POISED group's work. They asked for a new, formal charter for the IAB and IETF to enshrine these procedures, but gave temporary approval to move forward immediately. The new selection process began in January 1993, with the first round of nominations expected by February 1993. The new IESG and IAB members would take office at the March 1993 IETF meeting.

While governance was being reformed, the original technical problems the IAB and IESG had been debating (IP addressing, routing, and later IPng) continued in their own working groups. The POISED reforms separated the structural governance questions from technical architecture questions, allowing both to proceed.
sections.eli5: The Internet Society said yes to the new process. By March 1993, the first leaders chosen by the new system took office.

references.text: Chapin, S. and C. Huitema, 'The Internet Standards Process', October 1992
